reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed lab work needs surface-modified clays that must be prepared or sourced with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Modified clays remove HAB cells far better than natural clay and are widely used in China, but no percent is given.
reasons.cost: Lab-scale modified clay trials are roughly $150-500.
reasons.environment: Clay is applied at 4-10 t/km^2, settles to the seabed and is never retrieved, despite the authors' no-harm claim.

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed test is a jar/settling-column test with natural clay, but the target cultures (K. brevis, Heterosigma) are purchased, toxin-producing organisms needing a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Removal was 97% in lab and 90% in settling columns but fell with scale and flow (68% Florida mesocosms, 41% in a 20 cm/s flume); Korean 90-99% field figures are uncontrolled secondhand reports.
reasons.cost: Clay is cheap, but two HAB cultures plus media and a fluorometer or counting setup run about $150-500.
reasons.environment: Clay persists on the bottom and cell mortality and benthic impacts were studied as concerns.

reasons.reproducibility: Culture-tube screening of clays is simple, but G. breve is a brevetoxin producer.
reasons.effectiveness: Twelve of 26 clays removed >90% of G. breve at 0.25 g/L in triplicate vs sinking-corrected controls, but no clay beat 40% on Aureococcus unless dispersed, and cells can regrow at low loadings.
reasons.cost: Clays are cheap, but two CCMP cultures and in vivo fluorescence measurement put it at about $150-500.
reasons.environment: Clay persists and low doses may just move live cells to the bottom where they regrow.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs 48 adult blue crabs in tanks, PAC-modified clay and toxic K. brevis.
reasons.effectiveness: Randomised tanks (n = 12 per treatment) showed 95% cell removal at 24 h and 98% at 48 h vs untreated K. brevis, though settled cells were not shown dead.
reasons.environment: Clay dropped pH to 7.25 vs 7.86 for ~72 h and did not lower water-column brevetoxin; no crab harm was detected, but K. brevis alone killed only 1 of 12 crabs, so power was low, and clay stays in sediment.

reasons.reproducibility: 1,400 L mesocosms with a Sarasota Bay benthic community are far beyond school scale.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.2 g/L MC II removed 57% at 8 h and 95% at 48 h in triplicate 1,400 L tanks against untreated K. brevis controls.
reasons.environment: No benthic harm in 72 h, but carbonate chemistry shifted, some brevetoxin analogs rose and clay persists.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs PSP-toxic Alexandrium, a custom oxidized modified clay and toxin analysis.
reasons.effectiveness: PMPS-modified kaolin removed >95% of A. pacificum from the water column within 3 h in triplicate vs control, but >70% of cells turned into pellicle cysts and some viable cells in the floc kept releasing toxin.
reasons.cost: Kaolin and Oxone-type PMPS are cheap, but a toxic Alexandrium culture and PST analysis put it at $500-5,000.
reasons.environment: Toxins shifted to less toxic analogues, but viable cells and cysts in the settled floc kept secreting toxin and the clay (about 20x the stated PMPS dose) stays in sediment.

reasons.reproducibility: Jar tests with commercial clays and a Microcystis culture are a clear bench protocol.
reasons.effectiveness: At 0.7 g/L six materials (talc 97.6%, kaolinite 93.9%, etc.) topped 90% in 8 h, but at 0.2 g/L only sepiolite did, 14 clays were <50%, cells were in saline not lake water and replication is not stated.
reasons.cost: Clays and a culture are about $50-150.
reasons.environment: Clay-algae floc is left in the sediment; effects not assessed.

reasons.reproducibility: Test tubes and 1 L cylinders are simple, but it needs bloom water, PAC and lanthanum-modified bentonite.
reasons.effectiveness: PAC plus ballast removed 97 +/- 1.8% of chlorophyll-a, 20-60x lower than controls.
reasons.cost: PAC and lanthanum bentonite plus bloom sampling are roughly $150-500.
reasons.environment: PAC raised extracellular microcystin 3.5-6x, bottom-layer toxin rose up to 8x, and lanthanum persists.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs toxic K. mikimotoi, rotifers, mussels and tissue histology.
reasons.effectiveness: 0.1 g/L PAC-modified clay removed 81 ± 2.3% of K. mikimotoi in 2 h (triplicate), a single species and short settling test.
reasons.time: The 81% removal was measured after 2 h of settling.
reasons.environment: Little mussel impact at 0.1 g/L, but gill and digestive-gland damage at 0.5-1.0 g/L (one tank per dose), and clay-only rotifers died earlier (78 h vs 122 h).

reasons.reproducibility: Clearance-rate trials with loess, shellfish and Rhodomonas food are doable with a sponsor.
reasons.effectiveness: Does not measure HAB removal at all; it tests clay harm to filter feeders.
reasons.cost: Several shellfish species plus loess are roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Short-term feeding trials give results the same day.
reasons.environment: Loess cut scallop clearance even at 0.01 g/L; authors urge 'extreme caution'.

reasons.reproducibility: Needs a rainbow-trout gill cell line (RTgill-W1) and ichthyotoxic cultures.
reasons.effectiveness: Loess, zeolite, PAC and PAC-clays did not reduce toxicity; only high-swelling bentonite removed 100% at 0.1 g/L.
reasons.environment: Bentonite clay persists; efficacy and side-effects are clay-specific.

reasons.reproducibility: Typical reviewed trials use toxic Alexandrium with PAC-modified kaolinite.
reasons.effectiveness: Lab trials report ~75-99% removal at 0.2-1 g/L, but authors doubt scaling to blooms of hundreds of km^2.
reasons.cost: A lab trial with modified clay is roughly $150-500.
reasons.time: Duration not reported; scored conservatively at 4-7 days.
reasons.environment: Cyst formation rose to 17.9-24.6% with clay dose (seeding future blooms), and clay persists.
